title: Delegated Identity and Credential Brokering
summary: Work through Delegated Identity and Credential Brokering.

blocks.md: This lesson follows **Delegated Identity and Credential Brokering** in *Agent Security* (Vol III).

blocks.source: Vol III, Agent Security, § Delegated Identity and Credential Brokering
blocks.md: Enforcing the release and evidence rules of a later section requires knowing whose authority backs each outbound request. When the repair worker fetches source code from a private repository or submits a patch for review, attaching the requesting developer's personal token or a shared automation service account exposes every other repository and production service those credentials unlock. A misdirected call can then reach resources that have nothing to do with the active bug fix.

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Action-bound approval matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: Human approval binds to a digest of the canonical, host-resolved action, is presented out of band with the agent's explanation labeled untrusted, and is re-verified with its preconditions immediately before dispatch.

questions.q: The section **Delegated Identity and Credential Brokering** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Human approval binds to a digest of the canonical, host-resolved action, is presented out of band with the agent's explanation labeled untrusted, and is re-verified with its preconditions immediately before dispatch.

When an agent acts for a requester, effective permission is the intersection of requester rights, service principal, task grant, and issuer and receiver policy, with identities taken from the runtime's task record, never from prompt text.

Instructions, tool definitions, the request, and every observation are serialized into one token sequence in which no position carries enforced privilege, so injection is structural and exposure grows with every untrusted read.
A quarantined reader keeps raw untrusted text out of the planner and typed handles keep untrusted bytes out of context, but a schema-valid field is still an untrusted claim, not evidence.
